Fateme Hejazi,1 Narges Tavangar,1 Ali Saber,2 Mohammad Saeid Moeinfar1,3 1Student Research Committee, School of Medicine, Kashan University of Medical Sciences, Kashan, Iran; 2Department of Medical Ethics, School of Medicine, Kashan University of Medical Sciences, Kashan, Iran; 3Department of Medical Education, Faculty of Medicine, Mashhad University of Medical Sciences, Mashhad, IranCorrespondence: Mohammad Saeid Moeinfar, Kashan University of Medical Sciences, Pezeshk Blvd, Qutb-e Ravandi Blvd, Kashan, 87159-81151, Iran, Email [email protected]Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into clinical practice and medical education, yet research on AI and medical professional identity has largely evolved in parallel.Objective: To examine how AI is transforming fundamental components of medical professional identity and propose a framework for understanding its implications for professional identity formation in medical education.Methods: This narrative review synthesizes conceptual, empirical, and theoretical literature on AI, professional identity formation, and clinical practice through iterative literature searching and citation tracking. Peer-reviewed studies, regulatory data, and national survey reports were considered.Results: AI affects professional identity unevenly. Diagnostic, predictive, generative, and emerging autonomous systems most directly influence expertise, clinical reasoning, and professional autonomy, shifting physicians from exclusive holders of specialized knowledge toward validators of increasingly accessible but variably trusted information. Evidence of automation bias and reduced diagnostic performance highlights this transition. We conceptualize the divergence between the formal locus of clinical responsibility, which remains with physicians, and the functional locus of influence decisions, shared with AI, as the formal–functional gap (FFG). Its magnitude varies by AI configuration, identity component, and career stage, potentially placing trainees at risk of never-skilling and experienced physicians at risk of deskilling. Ethical responsibility, humanistic care, lifelong learning, and professional authority are affected more indirectly.Conclusion: AI-mediated professional identity change reflects a dynamic interaction between physicians’ developmental trajectories and evolving AI capabilities. Medical education should prioritize sustained expertise, clinical reasoning, professional autonomy, AI-interpretive judgment, and human oversight. The FFG remains a conceptual framework whose relationships require empirical validation.Plain Language Summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are now common in hospitals and medical schools. They help with diagnosing diseases, writing notes, and answering medical questions. While these tools can improve care, they also raise important questions about what it means to be a doctor.This review looked at how AI is changing the professional identity of physicians — the sense of who they are and what they are responsible for. We examined existing research, expert opinions, and real-world examples of AI use in medicine.We found that AI does not affect all parts of a doctor’s role equally. It has the strongest impact on medical knowledge, clinical decision-making, and professional independence. Doctors are shifting from being the only source of specialized knowledge to checking and interpreting information that AI systems provide. At the same time, legal responsibility for patient care still rests with the physician. We call this mismatch between formal responsibility and actual influence the “formal–functional gap”.This gap can create different risks. Medical students may never fully develop key skills if they rely too heavily on AI from the start. Experienced doctors may lose some of their skills over time through reduced practice. Other important parts of being a doctor — such as ethical responsibility, empathy, and lifelong learning — are affected more indirectly.These findings matter for medical education. Training programmes should protect doctors’ ability to think independently, teach them how to critically evaluate AI suggestions, and ensure that human oversight remains meaningful. The goal is not to reject AI, but to make sure that technology strengthens rather than weakens the core values and skills of the medical profession.Keywords: artificial intelligence, professional identity, professional identity formation, medical education, clinical reasoning, large language models

In roughly a decade, artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from initial development for natural images toward broader deployment in clinical practice.1 The United States (US) Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) list of authorized AI- and machine-learning-enabled devices grew from only 7 entries before 2010 to 343 by mid-2021, still heavily concentrated in radiology (70.3%) and cardiovascular (12.0%) specialties but no longer limited to them.2 Market reports indicate a high growth potential for AI in healthcare, with a reported 28% global compound annual growth rate and projections of significant market expansion.3 This diffusion is increasingly visible in physicians’ daily work: AI adoption in clinical practice is rapidly growing; by 2022, approximately 18.7% of US hospitals had integrated AI, and projections estimate that by 2025, 66% of physicians will incorporate AI into their clinical practice.4 By 2025, nearly two-thirds of US hospitals using Epic had adopted some form of ambient documentation tool, which listens to clinical encounters and drafts notes in real time.5

The consequential question is therefore not how many AI tools physicians use, but which cognitive and clinical tasks they perform and how many were previously considered constitutive of being a physician. AI is increasingly performing clinical tasks long regarded as the preserve of trained clinical judgment, though its opaque reasoning prevents clinicians from fully delegating diagnostic justification to these systems. A randomized trial in JAMA Network Open found that a large language model used alone scored higher on structured diagnostic reasoning than physicians with or without the model, although physician access to the model did not significantly improve their own reasoning scores.6 A 2025 meta-analysis of 30 studies similarly found substantial variation in large language model diagnostic accuracy by specialty and case complexity relative to clinicians.7 What distinguishes the current period is breadth rather than depth in one domain: expertise, documentation, and communication are being engaged simultaneously, warranting analysis through professional identity rather than narrower task-automation categories.

This lens matters because professional identity has consequences beyond academic description. A cross-sectional study of medical students found an inverse association between professional identity strength and burnout and mental health difficulties,8 while identity formation has been theorized as protective of physician wellbeing through meaning and belonging.9 Identity also underwrites medicine’s social contract with the public, formalized in charters linking physicians’ standing to competence, ethical conduct, and commitment to patient welfare.10 AI is capable of affecting several identity components simultaneously, therefore has implications beyond workflow efficiency.
